data.title: PEARL: Price Crash, Hashrate Decline - Some Profited While Others Suffered Losses and Left the Market
data.description:
Author: Jae, PANews

Pearl, a public blockchain that recently gained popularity due to its PoUW (Proof-of-Work) narrative and high mining rewards, has now encountered a market reversal.

Ten days ago, after the PEARL token hit an all-time high of $2.43, a massive influx of GPU computing power poured in. However, the market quickly reversed, with the price falling by more than 35% in just ten days, dropping to around $1.50. Following this, the network hashrate also dropped from its historical peak of 87.79 EH/s to 66.34 EH/s.

As the network hashrate continues to climb and mining difficulty continues to increase, the rewards per GPU have shrunk significantly, and more and more miners are beginning to complain that mining is becoming unprofitable.

Especially for miners renting GPUs, the high cost of computing power is eroding profits, with some latecomers even incurring losses. This round of dramatic fluctuations in computing power is like a mirror, reflecting the starkly different survival situations of different miner groups: some have their shutdown thresholds far below the coin price, ensuring a steady profit; others are already on the verge of breaking even, ready to exit at any moment. Competing with coin prices in terms of computing power is difficult: latecomers become the ones who "pay the price." In all PoW networks, price is always the guiding force for computing power, but there's a time lag between the signal reaching the computing power end. On October 21st, the daily gross profit per RTX 4090 card reached $11.4, far exceeding other GPU-based cryptocurrencies during the same period. The substantial profits drove a large amount of idle computing power to migrate across networks. The total network hashrate climbed from approximately 70 EH/s, peaking at 100.92 EH/s on October 27th. As of now, the total network hashrate has fallen back to 85.52 EH/s. The consequence of this hashrate migration was a disruption of the block generation rhythm. Pearl's target block generation time was originally 194 seconds, but during the peak of the hashrate frenzy, the actual block generation time was compressed to 160 seconds, passively generating nearly 40 extra blocks per day and adding millions of PEARL tokens to the secondary market daily. The fundamental contradiction lies in the fact that network difficulty adjustments consistently lag behind the influx of computing power. It wasn't until October 28th that the network difficulty climbed to a high of over 49M, a nearly 20% increase compared to the peak price of the coin that day, and remained at a high level. Meanwhile, the price of PEARL had already fallen to $1.75. This downward price movement coupled with the upward difficulty directly squeezed miners' profits, with the average daily gross profit per card declining by over 30% compared to its peak. High-cost computing power was the first to flee, and the total network computing power shrank by nearly a quarter within two days, only returning the block time to the baseline range designed by the protocol. In this race against time, the miners who rushed in first reaped the biggest profits, while those who were late to the game became the ones who ultimately paid the price when the market reversed. Same card, different accounts: retail investors counting money, mining farms switching to AI, short-term renters running away. The same card, held by different people, represents different businesses. Pearl's miner camp has already split into three distinct groups. Taking the mainstream graphics card RTX 4090 as an example, under the network difficulty and hashrate conditions on October 30th, a single card could produce approximately 4.2 PEARL per day. However, the capital costs and shutdown prices of different miners varied greatly, which determined their drastically different decision-making logic when facing this round of pullback. Home Miners: Sunk Costs Provide a Safety Buffer For most home miners, the graphics card is used for gaming or work, and the hardware purchase cost is already sunk; mining only requires additional electricity costs. Based on an average residential electricity price of $0.16/kWh, the daily electricity cost per card is only $3.84, corresponding to an average shutdown price as low as $0.87. In other words, as long as the average PEARL price remains above $0.87, they are making a pure profit. Even though the price of cryptocurrency has fallen by more than 35%, their daily net profit per SIM card remains stable at around $2.67, with a profit margin of about 70%. For home miners, this downturn isn't even a harsh winter; it's just a "tougher wind." As long as their cash flow remains positive, they will continue operating unless the price of cryptocurrency continues to plummet or a more profitable alternative emerges. Large-scale mining farms: It's not just about electricity costs, but also opportunity costs. Mining farms with industrial-grade electricity are the cost havens in the mining industry. With PPA protocol electricity prices as low as $0.05/kWh, and considering all shared costs such as site and maintenance, the total daily cost per SIM card is only $0.48, corresponding to an average shutdown price of only about $0.11. In terms of mining itself, their safety net is even thicker than that of home miners. However, there's another way to calculate the profits for mining farms. Hashrate is a universal asset. The cuPOW algorithm is compatible with AI inference tasks, allowing hardware to switch between mining and renting out AI hashrate at any time. Currently, the net cash flow from providing AI inference rental services for an RTX 4090 is approximately $0.35 per hour, equivalent to about $8.4 per day. On October 30th, the daily revenue per PEARL mining card fell to $6.51, already lower than the return from AI inference rental. Rather than risking a decline in coin prices by continuing to mine, it's more profitable to steadily collect hashrate rental fees. Therefore, some mining farms with lower risk tolerance have begun to actively withdraw, shifting their hardware to AI rental services or other more competitive PoW networks, becoming one of the driving forces behind the peak and subsequent decline in hashrate. For mining farms, opportunity cost and the return per unit time of GPUs are two equally important financial indicators. Cloud computing power renters: the main force behind this round of drastic fluctuations in computing power. In this wave of computing power exodus, short-term computing power renters were the most resolute escapees. They do not own any physical hardware; they only rent computing power on platforms like Vast.ai by the hour, mining, withdrawing, and selling on the same day, earning the intraday price difference. Based on an average rental fee of $0.35 per hour, the average daily cost is as high as $8.4, corresponding to an average shutdown price of about $2. When the price of cryptocurrency plummeted to $1.75, renters were already collectively incurring losses. Cloud computing power has no sunk costs; the decision to shut down is made in an instant. During the three days of sharp drop in computing power, the vast majority of those leaving were short-term "speculators." However, some cloud mining miners had signed non-refundable long-term contracts for weekly or monthly periods. Having already paid the rental fees, they could recoup some of their losses by continuing to mine. If the price of Pearl recovers, there might be a chance to break even. Therefore, some long-term miners are still holding on. Ninety percent of computing power is idle; liquidity and centralization risks loom large. Besides the internal problem of declining computing power, Pearl also faces external threats such as questioning its narrative. Pearl paints a picture of "mining = doing useful AI computing," but a huge gap exists between reality and ideal. 90% of PoUW computing power is idle. Pearl's main selling point is "replacing invalid hashing with AI computing, making mining commercially valuable." But in reality, this vision remains on paper. Scholar Abhinaba Basu's empirical research, after sampling and analyzing 8,012 active mining machines, points out that over 90% of the network's computing power is not running any deep learning models or real inference tasks, but is simply continuously computing meaningless random matrices. The reason is that connecting to real AI inference requires handling context scheduling, model weight loading, and network I/O overhead, which can cause a 10%-30% decrease in the effective computing power of mining machines. Under the rule that block rewards depend solely on hash difficulty, the optimal choice for rational miners is to abandon real demand and simply run random matrices. The so-called "useful workload" is largely "garbage mining." The potential selling pressure in the secondary market: The continuous release of tokens also brings considerable selling pressure to the secondary market. Pearl currently produces approximately 1 million tokens daily. Based on market prices, the daily new miner selling pressure exceeds $1.55 million, with an annualized inflation exceeding $565 million, approaching the protocol's circulating market capitalization. Spot trading is concentrated on a few small and medium-sized exchanges, with an average daily spot trading volume of less than $10 million. Miner selling pressure alone accounts for nearly 20% of the daily trading volume, indicating limited market depth. Once a concentrated sell-off occurs, the weak buying depth can easily trigger a liquidity crunch. Furthermore, during the low-difficulty period of the first six days after the mainnet launch, nearly 122 million tokens were mined across the network, accounting for over 35% of the circulating supply. This early release lacked lock-up restrictions and remains a significant obstacle to the secondary market. The centralized nature of Pearl's hashrate also exposes potential cybersecurity risks. On-chain data shows that the single mining pool Kryptex has consistently held nearly half of the network's hashrate, approaching the 51% attack threshold. For PoW systems that rely on hashrate competition to maintain network security, a single mining pool controlling an excessively high proportion of hashrate means the network is more vulnerable to risks such as hashrate concentration, transaction censorship, and potential attacks. Pearl is now at a critical juncture: as the mining boom fades and the hype cools, its ability to attract sufficient real-world AI inference demand and generate commercial value from "useful work" will be crucial to its long-term prospects. For miners and investors, this ebb and flow of computing power also offers a valuable lesson. More important than chasing short-term gains is understanding one's cost basis. In the crypto industry, market conditions determine the upper limit of returns, while costs determine whether an individual can weather the cycle.

data.title: 2008 Revisited: A Comprehensive Guide to Wall Street's Hottest Trading AI, CDS
data.description:
Author: Bao Yilong, Wall Street Insights

As AI giants aggressively expand by burning through cash, the credit market has sounded the alarm. The CDS spreads of chipmakers like Broadcom and Nvidia have surged by over 170% in six months. While 10 core AI companies, including Google and Amazon, only account for 8% of the investment-grade index, they carry 16% of the implied credit risk. Chip manufacturers are transforming from tech companies into "centralized lending institutions," with CDS trading volume surging by over 1900% year-on-year.

Barclays released a comprehensive report on the credit default swap (CDS) market for AI-related companies, pointing out that with the significant expansion of capital expenditures, the credit risk of AI-related companies has undergone a significant repricing, with both CDS trading volume and spreads showing a sharp upward trend.

... On October 29, a Barclays report pointed out that 10 core AI companies, including hyperscale cloud service providers such as Google, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft, and Oracle, as well as chip manufacturers such as AMD, Broadcom, and Nvidia, currently account for only 8% of the CDX investment-grade index, but already represent 16% of the index's implied credit risk. Barclays emphasized that the credit risk of these ten companies has increased over the past six months and is currently near the upper limit of their six-month fluctuation range.

（AI Group: Comparison of the current 5-year CDS six-month interval）

This means that investors holding this investment-grade index have been passively taking on a significant amount of volatility risk in the AI ​​sector. Furthermore, the basis between CDS and cash bonds of these core AI companies has turned positive, meaning the cost of purchasing default protection has exceeded the additional returns from holding these corporate bonds.

According to Bloomberg, this anomaly is primarily due to a large number of institutions that do not hold related bonds (such as hedged equity funds and banks) buying CDS in large quantities to hedge against the huge AI capital expenditures and related loan risks.

This technical fluctuation, in its logic of credit hedging and basis distortion, is remarkably similar to that of 2008. Back then, many institutions (such as hedge funds and investment banks) that did not hold subprime mortgage bonds, driven by a bearish macroeconomic outlook or risk aversion, bet on default risk by purchasing CDS protection. This concentrated buying of naked hedging derivatives pushed CDS spreads extremely high, even exceeding the credit spreads of the underlying bonds, directly causing the CDS-cash bond basis to turn positive. As Barclays released this report, the financing needs of leading technology companies continued to put pressure on the market. Recently, Microsoft launched a bond issuance of over $25 billion, Amazon added over $48 billion in long-term debt in a single quarter, and Broadcom plans to raise up to $21 billion early next year. These massive financings further increased market hedging demand, causing the CDS costs for related companies to reach record highs.

Cardholder Credit Characteristics Shift, Spreads Widen Significantly

In this wave of credit repricing, the widening of CDS spreads for chipmakers has been the most significant.

Six months ago, Broadcom, AMD, and Nvidia's CDS spreads were among the lowest in their category, hovering around 40 basis points.

(AI Group 5-Year CDS, Six Months Ago vs. Now, Sorted by Six-Month Change)

However, the CDS spreads of these three companies have now jumped to the top, with Broadcom's 5-year CDS surging 258% in six months, AMD rising 177%, and Nvidia rising 172%. In contrast, Microsoft, rated AAA, has only risen 20%.

Barclays noted in its report that as chip suppliers begin to offer loans to customers to purchase their chips (i.e., supplier financing), the credit market has begun to view these companies as lenders with highly concentrated loan ledgers.

For example, Broadcom stepped in to provide a guarantee after banks raised concerns about Anthropic's $63 billion chip deal. Based on this, Barclays recommends buying Broadcom's 5-year CDS protection as a macro strategy to hedge against broader AI financing pressures. The positive basis and hedging demand drive a surge in trading volume. The positive basis between CDS and cash bonds is the most significant technical feature of the current AI credit market. Over the past year, the basis for non-AI companies in the CDX investment-grade index has remained largely negative, meaning the CDS spread was lower than the bond spread. However, the basis for the AI ​​sector has risen by about 50 basis points and turned positive. This positive basis is particularly evident among chipmakers and Oracle.

(The CDS-cash bond basis for AI companies has now turned positive, while the basis for non-AI companies remains negative)

This structural change is accompanied by an explosive growth in trading volume. As of October 23, the four-week average weekly trading volume for hyperscale cloud service providers reached approximately $6 billion, a surge of approximately 740% year-over-year; the weekly trading volume for chip manufacturers reached $3 billion, a dramatic increase of 1900% year-over-year.

(The CDS-cash bond basis for AI companies has now turned positive, while the basis for non-AI companies remains negative)

This structural change is accompanied by an explosive growth in trading volume. As of October 23, the four-week average weekly trading volume for hyperscale cloud service providers reached approximately $6 billion, a surge of approximately 740% year-over-year; the weekly trading volume for chip manufacturers reached $3 billion, a surge of 1900% year-over-year.

... (CDS trading volume for hyperscale cloud service providers and semiconductor companies has increased significantly.) Open interest data also confirms the continued inflow of funds. The net notional value of open interest for hyperscale cloud service providers has more than doubled from approximately $5 billion a year ago to $20 billion, while that of chip manufacturers has increased from approximately $1.9 billion to $8.6 billion.

(Open interest in AI-related contracts has increased from approximately $7 billion a year ago to over $28 billion currently)

These 10 AI companies currently account for nearly 14% of all open interest in single-name CDS contracts in the Americas, far higher than the 4% a year ago.

Curve curve divergence highlights individual stock differences in trading strategies

Through analysis of the 3-year and 5-year spreads in the CDS curve, Barclays pointed out pricing anomalies in some companies.

For example, Amazon and Google's 5-year CDS levels are comparable (80-81 basis points), but Amazon's 3s5s curve (3-year to 5-year spread) is only 18 basis points, which appears too flat. (The absolute value of the current 3s5s CDS curve and its percentage of 5-year CDS) Barclays believes this may be related to buying pressure from a term loan from Amazon in June and recommends buying Amazon 5-year protection or building a steepening trade portfolio. The subsequent financial data confirmed the necessity of hedging. Amazon announced that its free cash flow consumption reached $33.5 billion in the third quarter, and capital expenditures reached $77.3 billion. As the most liquid CDS underlying asset in the market, Oracle's basis is at a high level in the sample. (Comparison chart of the current CDS-cash bond basis position within the one-year period) Barclays recommends selling Oracle's 5-year basis, that is, selling bonds maturing in 2032 while simultaneously selling CDS for protection, in order to bet on the convergence of the basis. Previously, Oracle announced it would cap additional financing for the next few years at $20 billion. Intel is the only company in the sample with a negative basis (-14 basis points) and a relatively steep curve, primarily due to its lack of deep involvement in its peers' supplier financing models. However, after releasing weak earnings guidance, its stock price experienced its largest single-day drop since 1982. A microcosm of the high-yield market: CoreWeave's high default protection costs. Beyond investment grade, CoreWeave, as the only directly related AI company CDS in the CDX high-yield index, has become a unique window into observing the credit risk of data center and emerging cloud service providers. Currently, CoreWeave's 5-year CDS uses a "points upfront" pricing method, reaching 15.5 points. This pricing model, typically used for distressed debt, highlights the market's high level of vigilance regarding its risk.

(CoreWeave 5-year CDS, quoted in prepaid points)

Data shows that CoreWeave's weekly CDS trading volume has increased from $32 million a year ago to $302 million, and open interest has increased to $850 million.

(CoreWeave's weekly trading volume has risen to $302 million from $32 million a year ago, with open interest increasing to $850 million.) Despite analysts maintaining an "overweight" rating on CoreWeave bonds, its high upfront cost of 15.5 basis points for default protection indicates that the CDS market is pricing in the potential default risks of its business model more rigorously.

data.title: Anonymous Interviews with Leading Investors and Entrepreneurs: Who is Pressuring Who to Pursue Consensus?
data.description:
Author: BlockBeats

“VCs now only invest in consensus.”

Over the past period, we've spoken with many entrepreneurs, and this is a phrase many people mention. But with investors, we hear more of the sentiment, “There are too few good projects.”

These two statements sound like mutual accusations, but looking at the bigger picture, this confrontation is nothing new in the industry. Group buying, bike sharing, new consumption, big data models—every round has a direction that everyone is investing in, and every round has a group of entrepreneurs complaining that they're not riding the wave.

The difference this time is that there's more money, and the field is more crowded. According to statistics, in the first half of 2026, the domestic AI sector raised 307.682 billion yuan, exceeding the total for 2025, with about 80% flowing into big data models and embodied intelligence.

During the same period, many AI application entrepreneurs were unclear about what stage their products needed to reach before securing the next round of funding. Why does money always seem to flow in the same direction? Why does a sector go from hot to cold in just a few months? Who ultimately decides what to invest in? These questions are difficult to answer frankly in public. Investors have LPs, partners, and portfolio companies behind them; entrepreneurs face the next round of funding, investors, and peers. We wanted to hear what those on both sides of the table had to say privately. Besides having long one-on-one conversations with several entrepreneurs, we also hosted an offline meetup at the end of October, inviting some leading investors to share their insights anonymously. After these discussions, it was difficult to pin the blame on any one party. Young investors have their own performance evaluations, partners have their own fears, LPs want to see an exit, and the only exit option is almost always an IPO; while entrepreneurs, to survive, can only gravitate towards trending topics. Everyone in their position has made reasonable choices, and when these choices are combined, it becomes everyone chasing a consensus. No one genuinely enjoys chasing consensus, yet most people do. To allow everyone to speak freely, we have anonymized all content, removing the interviewees' names, institutions, and projects and details that could reveal their identities. Quotes have been edited without altering their original meaning. "The entire capital world is a giant game of musical chairs." "Many executives at large companies are forced into entrepreneurship. For them, the most important thing is to keep their status." "Has anyone here seen Carry? The primary market isn't a place for young people to get rich." "If you miss the next super platform, you won't be able to join top-tier institutions in the next era." "My biggest feeling throughout my career is that I feel like I'm being lied to every single moment." "Talent density won't suddenly change. It's just that the focus of capital has selected a group of people at this point in time, making them the chosen ones. It's really just a lottery." "Funding and all that stuff is fake." "The most important metrics for a company are whether it can survive and how much value it can create." "The FOMO (Fear of Missing Out) level of each fund's partners is more exaggerated than I imagined." "You always have to find a piece of shit-flavored chocolate to eat." "There are probably no more than 10 funds that have truly made big money in this wave of large-scale models." In many institutions, young investors basically don't earn carry. An entrepreneur developing AI applications described this situation to us: promotions and year-end bonuses in many institutions largely depend on how many projects are pushed to the investment decision committee and receive a term sheet; investors themselves may not stay in the institution for long, and even if the company goes public, they won't receive much excess return. "If you push 10 projects and get term sheets, you'll have your return for the year. What happens to the company afterward is irrelevant." According to this entrepreneur, based on this incentive system, the easiest projects to push are those with the least resistance to getting approved—in other words, projects that everyone approves of. Going up another level, most institutions conduct top-down sector research; very few institutions truly only look at people. And what sector research seeks is precisely "someone to take over later." According to Carta statistics, as of the end of Q1 2025, the median DPI for US VC funds established in 2017 was only 0.27; among funds established in 2019 and 2020, only 37% and 30% respectively distributed money to LPs. Preqin listed the top 10 USD VC funds with the highest DPI (Depth Income Per Investor) among those established between 2015 and 2020 that primarily invested in China. Of these, only 4 returned more money to their LPs than their principal. The industry itself is also shrinking. Data from the Asset Management Association of China shows that as of the end of April 2026, there were 11,248 existing private equity and venture capital fund managers, more than 800 fewer than at the beginning of 2025. According to media reports, many institutions are first cutting year-end bonuses, citing difficulties in exiting projects; some institutions have also reduced salaries by 20% for junior staff and 30% for middle staff. At Beating's Meetup, an investor asked if anyone had seen Carry before; after a few seconds, someone said they might have. According to this investor, the primary market is unlikely to make young people rich anymore. When asked what they're after and what their initial motivation is for investing in projects now, the answer was simply, "It's out of passion." Investors don't deny the pressure to invest. Few institutions explicitly assess the number of investments, but the anxiety of seeing peers invest rapidly is real. Some openly admit that investing in projects with a resume-building element is "the norm." The bar certainly exists, but it fluctuates with the popularity of the sector. If the sector is important enough and the team barely meets the requirements, then it's time to fire. One investor admitted that there are quite a few projects they're not satisfied with but have to invest in, "You always have to find a piece of chocolate that tastes like shit." The pressure isn't just on young people. The same investor frankly stated that the FOMO of the founding partners in this round is more severe than he expected, with veteran investors being more willing to gamble. The reasons are twofold: first, the fear of missing out on the super platforms of the AI ​​era, which would prevent them from joining top-tier institutions in the next era; second, the distance from the front lines, meaning there's always a delay in relaying changes seen on the front lines to partners. Entrepreneurs see things from a different perspective. One entrepreneur, who spoke with roughly 30% to 50% of top-tier dollar funds, felt that veterans with over a decade of experience were generally very strong, able to see through the underlying logic and provide genuine feedback; those chasing trends were investment managers with only a few years in the industry, "who don't understand business or products, only transactions." The consensus in the AI ​​field generally comes from four sources. First, pronouncements from industry leaders. One entrepreneur recalled that in February of this year, a batch of OpenClaw-like agent products suddenly became popular, starting with Wang Huiwen saying on Jike that he really wanted such projects. Secondly, there's the data seen by leading institutions, but "the data may be inflated." Last year, dollar-denominated institutions noticed a type of AI interactive content product that was cheap to acquire customers and had good second-day retention rates. Soon, some companies were comparing themselves to the previous generation of short video platforms in their investment application materials. Thirdly, there's the technological narrative; the world model craze is largely related to Fei-Fei Li and a group of recognized researchers. Fourthly, there's the industry research conducted by each VC. Once these forces combine, from reaching a consensus to actually investing, "it might only take a month." This year's OpenClaw is a good example. One entrepreneur observed that within a month, almost all VCs had scouted out teams in related fields; if the people were good and the direction was right, they would be invested in.

OpenClaw Hong Kong Meetup｜Image source: X

But after the window closed, the situation for those who came later was completely different. That entrepreneur had a friend who, along with several other "star projects" at the time, started making interactive content around the same time. His team wasn't based in Beijing, Shanghai, or Shenzhen, and he missed that round of financing.

But after the window closed, the situation for those who came later was completely different. That entrepreneur had a friend who, along with several other "star projects" at the time, started making interactive content. His team wasn't based in Beijing, Shanghai, or Shenzhen, and he missed that round of financing.

Once those two companies reached a consensus, when they went to raise funds again, the most frequent question from investors became, "How will you beat them?" Around 2010, during the "Group Buying Wars," there were over 5,000 group buying websites. In 2016, with shared bikes, about 80 bike-sharing apps could be found in Android app stores; two years later, Mobike was acquired, and long queues formed outside ofo for deposit refunds. In 2021, the new consumption boom saw 842 financing deals totaling over 90 billion yuan; a Changsha snack brand saw its valuation increase by about 500 times in 10 months, only to lay off 40% of its employees the following year. Compared to these, the window for AI opened even faster and closed even faster. The window for AI applications closed at the end of April this year. This was the timeframe given by investors at a Meetup, and one entrepreneur felt that this year was the year with the lowest enthusiasm for application investment. Both sides gave almost identical reasons: there were no new narratives, and the models were powerful enough that they could handle many tasks required by applications themselves. Furthermore, looking back at the past returns on investment for software applications, the returns weren't impressive, and the rapid progress of AI coding further compressed the potential for application growth. When the window of opportunity tightens, even signed term sheets (TSs) can be withdrawn. Before the Spring Festival this year, a fund was preparing to invest in a video generation company. In mid-February, a major company released a new generation video model, and a fund tore up its TS, citing "definitely can't compete." During sector rotation, projects that were considered for investment one month might be abandoned the next. The most common explanation from funds is that their money hasn't been secured yet. One investor said, "You can do whatever you want before the money is settled. Although entrepreneurs can't afford to wait." This is the exact opposite of the pace a year ago. At the height of the boom, some institutions would make payments the day after meeting the founder, and some founders had millions of dollars deposited into their personal accounts before their companies were even registered. Currently, signing an agreement quickly takes about one or two months, but payment can take even longer. "Dollar funds only invest after a consensus is reached," is the assessment of one entrepreneur. We brought this up on Meetup, and a dollar fund investor replied, "Overall, I think so." This investor explained it by the decision-making mechanism. The final decision rests with the partners, and since each partner receives similar information, has similar industry backgrounds, and has worked on similar projects, it's not surprising that they reach similar conclusions. However, this investor doesn't believe they are chasing consensus. "We're not looking for non-consensus; we're looking to lead the consensus. The best scenario is that today I understand it, a few others understand it, and in two months everyone understands it and wants to invest." If, after two months, people still don't understand it, the project is in trouble. This kind of consensus, simply put, is actually a "consensus that's still cheap." Benchmark co-founder Andy Rachleff once said that to make big money, you need to be non-consensus and right. Howard Marks of Oaktree Capital also said that consensus isn't necessarily wrong; excess returns come from when the consensus is wrong, and you happen to be right. This "consensus that's still cheap" is different from both of these statements; it's closer to the beauty pageant that Keynes described in 1936, where judges had to guess which face others would find most beautiful.

1930 Beauty Pageant Group Photo｜Image Source: Maurer

However, the reasons for this situation are also very realistic. For an AI company to grow, it often needs to raise several rounds of funding. Whether or not someone will take over the next round is more critical than whether the investment in the current round is right. In May of this year, an entrepreneur met with a seasoned investor who doesn't usually chase trends. The investor liked their team very much but gave a sober assessment, saying that there are no more than 10 investors who can invest in AI to C applications this year. Even if this round of investment goes in and the company does well, if the next round of funding doesn't come in, the company will still die.

So, entrepreneurs are left with only two paths. They can stick to their direction, leave fundraising to luck, and gamble on which of dozens of VCs will take a liking to them; or they can gravitate towards mainstream trends to reduce the probability of fundraising obstacles. Most people chose the latter. The entrepreneur used the consumer industry as an example to illustrate the value of non-consensus. Pop Mart's earliest funding came from angel investor Mai Gang and Qifu Capital's first fund, which was only around 100 million yuan. Sequoia Capital didn't enter until the pre-IPO stage. BaWangChaJi's two rounds of financing in 2021, totaling over 300 million yuan, were invested in by XVC, Fosun, and Congbi Qiushi. These investors weren't considered top-tier in the VC circle at the time. Unable to secure mainstream projects, they had to look for things outside the consensus, and later, they actually achieved excess returns.

The giant cup at the opening of BaWangChaJi in the Philippines

Investors at the Meetup also admitted that small funds and solo GPs are more likely to invest in non-consensus projects because consensus projects are too expensive for them to invest in. As for institutions that claim to "like to invest in non-consensus projects," the entrepreneur disagreed: "They don't invest in non-consensus projects; they only invest in consensus projects, just packaged as non-consensus projects."

The Chosen Ones

Every year, there are favored groups in the AI ​​industry. One entrepreneur observed that this year it's PhDs from good labs, and last year it's people working on smart hardware.

The Chosen Ones

Talent density doesn't change year by year; what changes is the attention from capital. Those who receive that attention become the chosen ones of the year—it's essentially more like a lottery. The "world model" concept is a prime example. According to media statistics, by July of this year, there were over 30 domestic startups with "world models" as their core concept, raising over 26 billion yuan in total funding, with 7 becoming unicorns. At least 4 of the founders are born in the 2000s. In early October, Tian Keyu's company was reported to have completed nearly $30 million in funding, with a post-investment valuation of $200 million; it also deals with world models.

Li Feifei HAI Roundtable｜Image source: Stanford

According to one entrepreneur, VCs generally categorize entrepreneurs into three types. One type is those who have reached high-level positions in large companies by age 25, and will get investment no matter what they do; another type is those who are decent people, but not quite at that level, in which case the "business" becomes extremely important; and the third type is those who are incompetent, no matter how good their business is. Most entrepreneurs belong to the second type, and whether they can get funding largely depends on whether their direction overlaps with the focus of mainstream investors.

Investors also admit it's like a lottery, except the market rotates.

Investors also admit it's very much like a lottery, except the market also rotates.

When the market is booming, entrepreneurs with academic backgrounds are more sought after; when the market is slow, they are no longer the main players. Some investors suspect that some scholars who start businesses may not be motivated by a desire to build a great career, but simply by seeing their peers succeed and wanting the same high valuations. Someone at the event chimed in, "Some people see that even Tang Jie has succeeded, and they think, 'Why can't I?'" Zhipu, co-founded by Tsinghua University professor Tang Jie, listed on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange on January 8th this year, with an issue price of HK$116.2, and reached a high of HK$2980 in June. Another concern is the possibility of a fallback plan. A professor who fails in their startup can return to academia; many entrepreneurs, however, lose everything after failure. Investors generally have more faith in those with no backup plan, some even using a lack of determination as a veto factor. One entrepreneur put it more bluntly: "True entrepreneurs are those who are constantly starting new businesses; those who only start businesses when the timing is right are often those with good backgrounds and backup plans." Having a background in a large company is often seen as a plus. Investors reason that people from large companies are good at reporting upwards and can explain things more clearly to partners; moreover, the AI ​​generation hasn't escaped the mobile internet era, distribution is still controlled by a few large platforms, and product methodologies haven't changed. But this plus is becoming increasingly less of an advantage. An investor from a US dollar fund commented on entrepreneurs who came from several large companies, saying that some companies have many founders, but none have achieved outstanding success. Replicating their former employers' methodologies ultimately leads to direct competition with those same companies. Some founders use the presence of several high-level executives on their teams as a selling point, "but how much of the success achieved in large companies is given to you by the platform, and how much is truly your own?" Other companies are too comfortable, with almost no executives proactively starting their own businesses. One entrepreneur added another perspective, saying that many executives from large companies are forced to start their own businesses because they can't stay in their companies or are about to be laid off. For them, preserving their status is paramount, and aligning with mainstream trends is a natural choice. High-level executives with proven track records have lower financing costs, while the biggest challenge for young people is proving their traction to investors. The wolf is coming. Entrepreneurs and investors have very different views on "storytelling." Some entrepreneurs feel that jargon is useless, that investors are very smart, and that those who really need to work on their narratives are those who don't want to build a good product but just want to get a quick buck. In this entrepreneur's classification, those who ride the wave of trending topics are mainly "pseudo-entrepreneurs" whose mission is simply to become famous and then raise funds. Investors are much more wary. One investor said that his biggest takeaway from this industry is that he's constantly on guard against the other party lying. Both sides have clear objectives, trust is inherently difficult to build, and once someone has lied even once, they're immediately blacklisted. Another investor's perspective is more moderate: there are no perfect projects, and when it comes to making a decision, there's always the worry that a certain flaw will become a bigger problem; if a project is completely without reservation, it's either a genius or too good to be true. And how to judge a person still has no standard answer. Some investors will specifically ask entrepreneurs about the most difficult moments they've experienced, to see if they've truly reflected on their experiences, and they'll also ask what the entrepreneur wants to be ten years from now; but most of the time, the decisive feeling is simply "we get along well," and being willing to talk for hours. Top funds' investment decision materials have a framework, but at the execution level, everyone adds their own interpretation. That investor believes this is probably the only reason why venture capital is hard to be replaced by AI. The technology itself is even harder to judge. The more cutting-edge the AI ​​field—world models, embodied intelligence, underlying infrastructure—the fewer people there are who can truly evaluate the technological roadmap at the investment decision meeting. One investor also shared an example she experienced when looking at hard technology projects: a nuclear fusion project that failed to pass two investment decision meetings. The reason had nothing to do with technical knowledge; "the partners didn't understand it either, and no one present had a level higher than a university undergraduate." The PE professionals in the same field read numerous papers and conducted extensive research, but ultimately couldn't provide a convincing judgment on the roadmap selection; the decision still came down to investing in the people. When investors can't understand the technology, they can only rely on two things: the people involved and who else is investing. The latter is the source of consensus. Exit was the most discussed and also the most somber topic. One entrepreneur said that the fundamental difference between Chinese and American VCs lies in exits. In the US, there are numerous mergers and acquisitions; a young person can create a product, sell their company, and make money, and those who make money are willing to invest in venture capital. Here, however, the only way to exit is basically through an IPO.

Nasdaq Live Stream

According to statistics from PitchBook and NVCA, in 2025, among the exits of VC-backed companies in the United States, there were 62 IPOs and 995 M&A deals; as of the third quarter, 75% of the companies acquired that year had only raised a maximum of Series A funding.

Nasdaq Live Stream

According to statistics from PitchBook and NVCA, in 2025, there were 62 IPOs and 995 M&A exits of VC-backed companies in the United States; as of the third quarter, 75% of the companies acquired that year had only raised a maximum of Series A funding.

... AI companies in the US have another outlet: "talent acquisition." In 2024, Google brought the founding team of Character.AI back to the company for approximately $2.7 billion in licensing fees, and in 2025, it spent $2.4 billion to acquire the core team and technology license of Windsurf. In 2024, Microsoft took away most of the Inflection team for $650 million. In 2025, Meta spent $14.3 billion to acquire 49% of Scale AI. At the end of September this year, AMD announced the acquisition of World Labs for approximately $8.2 billion.

Su Zifeng and Li Feifei sign an agreement | Image source: World Labs

However, the data from Zero2IPO shows a different picture. In the first half of 2026, out of 2,503 exit cases in the equity investment market, 1,732 were IPO exits, and only 368 were M&A exits.

The door to listing is not something one can control.

In 2023, 313 companies listed on the A-share market, raising 356.4 billion yuan. On August 27th of that year, the China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC) proposed "temporarily tightening the pace of IPOs." In April 2024, new capital market regulations were introduced, reducing the number of new A-share listings to around 100, raising approximately 67.3 billion yuan—a ten-year low. Simultaneously, 425 companies that planned to list terminated their IPO plans. The Hong Kong stock market absorbed some of the burden. In March 2023, Chapter 18C of the Hong Kong Stock Exchange came into effect, allowing unprofitable specialized technology companies to list. In 2025, Hong Kong stocks raised HK$285.693 billion, regaining its position as the world's largest market. This January, Zhipu and MiniMax listed on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange.

HKVCA Venture Capital Forum｜Image source: HKEX × HKVCA Stage

However, the price trend in the secondary market was equally dismal. When we asked investors whether such stock prices would affect their continued investment in large-scale models, the answer was "definitely."

The path of mergers and acquisitions is being actively opened up by policy. In September 2024, the China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC) released six measures on mergers and acquisitions. In the first half of this year, M&A exits increased by 94.7% year-on-year, but the 368 deals still only accounted for about 20% of IPO exits. The path of cross-border M&A has been blocked again this year.

This exit structure directly determines what investors are willing to invest in. At Meetup, investors quoted a minimum valuation of at least several tens of times higher than their initial investment, starting at tens of billions, arguing that VCs aim to invest in 100 projects and earn a hundredfold return from just one. Companies with predictable buyers from the start, destined for valuations of only a few billion, such as those optimizing open-source software or framework tools, even if they could generate several times the return for investors, would struggle to pass IPO reviews. "Several times the return isn't enough." The only remaining exit strategy is an IPO, which requires a scale of tens of billions, necessitating several rounds of large-scale fundraising, each requiring someone to take over. What entrepreneurs call "passing the parcel" becomes, for investors, a no-go exit path. The Seven-Year Itch: Changes in USD funds represent the other end of this chain. Before the Meetup, we received an anonymous comment stating that USD funds are becoming increasingly "localized," with a different risk-taking capacity and willingness compared to the past. Investors present agreed that this is a trend, with more and more USD funds starting to raise RMB, and in terms of rules, pace, and boldness, they are becoming more and more like RMB funds. Based on the "5+2" lifespan, the USD funds that completed fundraising in 2021 and 2022 are almost ready to raise new funds again. This time, many LPs are looking at actual distributions, and there is significant differentiation within the industry. Some mentioned hearing about funds with a thousand-fold DPI, while others joked that they couldn't really tell others their DPI was only 0.1. Some investors estimate that no more than 10 funds may have truly made a fortune in this wave of large-scale model investments. The structure of dollar funds themselves has also changed. In June 2023, Sequoia Capital announced a regional split, completed in March 2024; GGV Capital also completed its split in 2024, renaming its Americas and Asia businesses Notable Capital and Granite Asia, respectively. Washington's restrictions on outbound investment took effect on January 2, 2025, limiting US funds from investing in semiconductor, quantum, and some AI companies in the US; the COINS Act, signed on December 18, 2025, further enshrined this mechanism in law. For funds that need dollar LPs, AI, which should have been the easiest story to tell, is now also the most compliance-sensitive area. Fundraising data reflects the same changes. According to Zero2IPO's statistics, RMB funds accounted for 97.8% of newly raised funds in 2025; only 33 foreign currency funds completed fundraising, totaling RMB 35.808 billion, a 36% decrease year-on-year. According to Zero2IPO founder Ni Zhengdong at the end of last year, foreign capital only accounted for about 2% of LPs. In the first half of this year, foreign currency funds raised approximately RMB 45.26 billion, a year-on-year increase of 122.5%, but only 19 funds completed fundraising, with the average size of each fund increasing by 145.9%, indicating that the money was concentrated in the hands of a few. Some investors are puzzled as to why global LPs are still unwilling to invest heavily in this area. Europe is declining, and no one wants to invest heavily in the Middle East; there are not many places where large sums can be placed. Another explanation is simple: the core issue is still the US-China relationship; LPs need to be able to withdraw their money when relations are tense. When money becomes tight, financial advisors (FAs) actually find it easier to do business. Investors say 2024 and 2025 will be the most profitable years for financial advisors (FAs). On-the-spot commissions are generally 3% to 5%, with close relationships sometimes yielding only 2%. However, discussions about off-the-spot kickbacks are shrouded in secrecy. When asked under what name this money is received, the answer is "all sorts of names. Friends, relatives, or relationships you can't quite put your finger on." In this interview, the only point of complete agreement between entrepreneurs and investors was on the "world model." One entrepreneur listed the world model as the "most narrative-driven" sector and described the process of the bubble bursting: everyone realized the business was unworkable, then strong evidence emerged, and the bubble burst. At the Meetup, when asked about the most overvalued sectors and areas they would resolutely avoid investing in, several investors cited the world model as their answer. Their dissatisfaction centers on the misnomer of the companies claiming to be world models. A plethora of companies doing 3D generation and real-time generation call themselves "world models," quoting valuations of hundreds of millions of dollars. Someone asked whether real-time video models qualify as world models, and whether they would consider investing if the companies didn't explicitly state they were creating world models. One investor replied, "If you don't call yourself a world model, don't ask for such a high valuation." After news of Tian Keyu's funding round broke, one investor said that while some had hoped for another wave of success with world models, that has now essentially hit the brakes. However, the good news is that investors still believe there will be another killer application. Without applications, models, computing power, and infrastructure become worthless. "If you don't believe in that, you can't invest in AI." "Preserving the Green Hills" A question was asked at a Meetup that, at first glance, seems unrelated to consensus: "Isn't the feedback cycle in the primary market so long frustrating?" It's common for an early-stage investment to take seven or eight years from investment to exit, and ten years isn't unusual. A relatively new investor said no, this industry is inherently long-term. The questioner followed up, saying that a long feedback cycle means you learn very slowly from past failures. The answer was even more surprising: you don't learn much from failures anyway; there are too many reasons for failure, and the more you review, the more confused you become. If in an industry, it takes ten years to see right and wrong, and failures teach almost nothing, how can those within it judge whether they're doing the right thing today? The latest and fastest signals are only the reactions of others, such as whether there's investment in the next round, whether the valuation has been inflated, and whether competitors are making moves in the same direction. In an industry where it takes a decade to determine right or wrong, consensus is one of the few pieces of feedback that can be obtained quickly. It provides reassurance, but it's also the easiest way to misjudge. Paul Graham wrote in his 2012 book, *Black Swan Farming*, that the best startup ideas often look like bad ideas at first glance; if they were clearly good, someone would have already done them. According to this logic, the few investments that truly determine a fund's success or failure are often those that no one believes in at the moment they are made. Bessemer Venture Partners in Silicon Valley maintains an "Anti-Portfolio" on its website, specifically listing companies they've missed out on, including Google, Facebook, Apple, and eBay, with explanations for why they didn't invest in each one. In an industry where everyone fears missing out, making a list of missed opportunities requires a touch of humor, but also a certain confidence. Entrepreneurs face the same problem, just in reverse. One entrepreneur, when starting out, treated VC opinions as the sole exam, meeting with each firm, recording their feedback, and adjusting their direction accordingly. Nine months later, the exam changed; it focused on user experience and data performance. "If I do well and get good feedback, I might be able to create consensus." There's a hint of ambition in this statement. Consensus must be created first, and that person often has to endure a period where no one believes in them. And the prerequisite for enduring, in this entrepreneur's words, is, "You have to ensure you're still on the table before the cycle begins." The young investor who said "failure doesn't teach you anything" was later asked about his most successful investment to date. He said he hadn't yet. "I invest because I believe it can accomplish things. If I didn't believe that, I wouldn't do it."

data.title: Bloomberg: Has Bitcoin truly matured after being accepted by Wall Street?
data.description:
Author: Teresa Xie, Bloomberg reporter; Translator: Jia Huan, ChainCatcher

Bitcoin is entering adulthood. At least in terms of age, it certainly is.

18 years ago, a person using the pseudonym Satoshi Nakamoto published a white paper envisioning a decentralized electronic payment system. This earliest form of cryptocurrency aimed to allow people to transfer money directly to each other without relying on banks or any central authority.

Now, Bitcoin will celebrate its 18th birthday this Saturday, and it's time to look back at how far it has come from Satoshi Nakamoto's original rebellious experiment. Many are familiar with this journey: some have made fortunes from it, others have had their relationships ruined; ecosystems have sprung up around it, and others have ultimately collapsed. Governments have bought it, celebrities have called it "rat poison," and many have debated its exact nature for years.

Along the way, Bitcoin has been declared dead and resurrected time and again; it has been rejected by the masses, but later gained a diverse range of supporters, including Wall Street.

This raises a crucial question: nearly 20 years after its inception, has Bitcoin truly matured, or is it merely feigning maturity? Wall Street Becomes a Supporter of Bitcoin "It has indeed come a long way," says Anastasia Melachrinos, Head of Growth at Kaiko. "Think about where Bitcoin first appeared—the dark web and forums. And in 18 years, we've gone from there to a completely new asset class." Bitcoin has made some unexpected friends and gained social acceptance, especially in recent years. Today, investors can invest in Bitcoin in various ways, including through products offered by Wall Street giants like BlackRock. BlackRock manages a $66 billion Bitcoin ETF (exchange-traded fund). Dozens of publicly traded companies have Bitcoin reserves on their balance sheets, and some of the world's wealthiest investors continue to praise it. The irony is clear. Bitcoin was originally created to challenge centralized finance; now, the very institutions it once sought to disrupt have become some of the strongest supporters of blockchain technology. Wall Street is accelerating its deployment of stablecoins, asset tokenization, and blockchain-based financial infrastructure, increasingly incorporating the technology into the financial system that Bitcoin initially attempted to bypass. There are many other examples, but few still evoke the idea of ​​rebelling against the traditional financial order. "Bitcoin's most fundamental significance lies in proving that value transfer can be completed without intermediaries," said Linda Jeng, Chief Legal and Policy Officer at Aave Labs. "Since then, Bitcoin has driven several rounds of development in digital finance. Technologies that were once on the fringes are becoming the new financial system." Volatility Declines, Price Movement Still Closely Follows US Stocks Looking at stability, Bitcoin has indeed made some progress in this area. The increasing popularity of ETFs has made investing in Bitcoin more convenient, which has contributed to a significant reduction in its previously dramatic price fluctuations. Earlier this month, its 30-day volatility fell to its lowest level in three years.

Chart caption: Bitcoin volatility declines, with its 30-day volatility falling to its lowest level in three years earlier this month. Source: Bloomberg.

This doesn't mean Bitcoin has completely shed its immature aspects; it still experiences significant ups and downs. Last October, a sudden sell-off resulted in the liquidation of a record $19 billion in leveraged positions in a single day, and this is far from the first time the crypto industry has experienced a boom-and-bust cycle.

This doesn't mean Bitcoin has completely shed its immature aspects; it still experiences significant volatility. Last October, a sudden sell-off led to the liquidation of a record $19 billion in leveraged positions in a single day, and this is far from the first time the crypto industry has experienced such a dramatic rise and fall.

Then there was the crypto winter of 2022, when in November, FTX, the crypto exchange founded by Sam Bankman-Fried, collapsed, wiping out over $2 trillion in market capitalization from crypto assets. Moreover, Bitcoin's price movements still mirror those of the US stock market. For example, it is highly correlated with the Nasdaq 100 index, indicating a lack of independence in its price movements. On its 18th birthday, the market lacked a celebratory atmosphere. As Bitcoin matured, it also lost some of its edge. It is no longer a rebel challenging tradition in the financial markets, nor a bold bet in the eyes of risk-takers, but rather an asset that ordinary investors would include in a balanced portfolio. Just last week, venture capital giant Andreessen Horowitz officially changed the name of its crypto fund from a16z Crypto to a16z Frontier. On the eve of Bitcoin's birthday, the market lacked much of a celebratory atmosphere. Based on current trends, this month may be Bitcoin's worst month since June. The upward momentum accumulated over the summer failed to continue, and the price is now hovering around $80,000. Supporters believe Bitcoin will soon return to $100,000, and may even eventually reach $1 million; critics, however, argue it's worthless. Anthony Scaramucci, founder of Skybridge Capital, first bought Bitcoin at $6,000 years ago and later at $16,000. He stated that he has always viewed this investment as a five-year bet. He predicts Bitcoin will double in the next five years, which, according to his calculations, equates to a compound annual return of approximately 15%. "Bitcoin is the benchmark of this industry," he said in an interview. "It will still exist long after you and I are gone."

data.title: Chainalysis: Sub-Saharan Africa Becomes the Fastest Growing Region for Crypto
data.description:
Author: Chainalysis; Translator: Luffy, Foresight News

Chainalysis, a data research institution in the crypto field, released its latest Global Crypto Adoption Report. The report's sub-Saharan Africa section mentions that the region's crypto economy grew by 13.4% year-on-year to $101 billion, the fastest growth rate globally. South Africa and Nigeria are the two core markets, experiencing a surge in demand for stablecoins, and the proportion of self-custodied wallets in the region is the highest globally. The local crypto adoption is mainly driven by real financial needs such as cross-border remittances and daily payments; the future market trend largely depends on regulatory clarity.

While sub-Saharan Africa is the smallest region in terms of global crypto economy size, it is also the fastest growing.

During the statistical period from July 1, 2025 to June 30, 2026, the region's cryptocurrency market grew by 13.4%, reaching $101 billion, with South Africa being the core driver of this growth. A very real reason behind the local cryptocurrency adoption is that many individuals and businesses still struggle to access affordable and reliable financial services. For ordinary people, cryptocurrency offers an alternative for managing funds and cross-border transfers; for businesses, it enables faster and lower-cost cross-border payments and settlements. In this region, the appeal of cryptocurrency lies not in creating entirely new financial products or speculative investment channels, but in addressing real-world financial pain points. As Mercy Emmanuel, Head of Stablecoin and Blockchain Business at Nigerian fintech company Flutterwave, stated, "For the African market, commercially viable innovations should simplify the frictions of existing financial activities, rather than deliberately increasing business complexity in order to use blockchain." South Africa and Nigeria dominate the regional market. South Africa and Nigeria dominate the sub-Saharan African crypto market, together accounting for more than three-quarters of the region's total crypto trading volume.

South Africa is the largest crypto economy in sub-Saharan Africa

However, the development paths of the two countries have clearly diverged. During the reporting period, South Africa's crypto economy reached $39.3 billion, a year-on-year increase of 52%, bucking the trend in a global bear market. Growth covered all statistical sectors, with the core drivers being cross-border P2P stablecoin transfers and fund flows related to various crypto services.

Nigeria's crypto market size is similar to South Africa's, reaching $38.1 billion, but transaction volume declined by 3% year-on-year.

The growth in centralized exchanges (CEXs) and the crypto services sector was offset by a 45% drop in decentralized exchange (DEX) trading volume and a 17% decline in cross-border P2P trading volume. Meanwhile, Nigeria ranked third globally in Chainalysis's grassroots crypto adoption index. South Africa and Nigeria account for three-quarters of the total crypto economy in sub-Saharan Africa. Looking at other countries, the trading activity of CEXs and DEXs profoundly impacts growth curves in various regions. Ghana's crypto market grew by 80% to $5.1 billion, with both CEX and DEX trading rising in tandem; Senegal's crypto trading volume surged 215% to $2.3 billion, with all growth coming from centralized exchanges. Conversely, Ethiopia's crypto market declined by 8% to $3.7 billion, primarily due to a contraction in DEX trading. These divergences illustrate the uneven pace of crypto adoption within the region. Smaller markets offer significant growth potential and can scale rapidly, but they also experience greater volatility and are highly susceptible to market fluctuations and regulatory changes. Regulation and market conditions can either accelerate adoption or directly disrupt growth momentum. Research shows that personal wallets account for a very high percentage of crypto funds in sub-Saharan Africa's crypto market, reflecting the unique adoption model there: individuals are the core holders and transferrs of crypto assets. During the statistical period, funds received by personal wallets accounted for 32.3% of the total amount received in the region, the highest proportion globally. This indicates that local users choose cryptocurrency largely for self-management of their funds, rather than relying on custodian intermediaries such as exchanges. Cross-border P2P transfers constituted the majority of these funds, accounting for 70.9% of the total amount received by personal wallets; domestic P2P transactions accounted for 18.5%; and transfers from crypto service platforms to personal wallets accounted for 10.7%.

One-third of crypto funds in sub-Saharan Africa flow to personal self-custodial wallets

Insufficient supply of custody services and regulatory uncertainty are important reasons why users prefer self-custodial wallets. Take Nigeria as an example: From 2021 to 2023, the Central Bank of Nigeria prohibited banks from providing services to crypto exchanges, and subsequently, the country also had tax disputes with leading international crypto platforms. These regulatory changes lead users to favor self-custodial services to avoid the risks brought about by future policy changes and market shutdowns.

One-third of crypto funds in sub-Saharan Africa flow to personal self-custodial wallets

Insufficient supply of custody services and regulatory uncertainty are important reasons why users prefer self-custodial wallets. For example, in Nigeria: From 2021 to 2023, the Central Bank of Nigeria prohibited banks from providing services to crypto exchanges, and subsequently, the country also had tax disputes with leading international crypto platforms. These regulatory changes make users inclined to self-custody, avoiding the risks brought about by future policy changes and market shutdowns.

Stablecoin trading volume in the region has increased sixfold, while Bitcoin inflows have shrunk by 60%. Stablecoins are rapidly defining the sub-Saharan African crypto market landscape. From 2022 to 2026, the amount of stablecoins received through P2P channels increased sixfold, from $2.3 billion to $14.6 billion; during the same period, Bitcoin inflows fell by 60%, from $36 billion to $14.6 billion.

Stablecoin trading volume increased sixfold, Bitcoin fell 60%

This change highlights the practical value of stablecoins: local individuals and businesses can use stablecoins to hold the value of foreign currencies such as the US dollar without opening foreign currency bank accounts. In sub-Saharan Africa, where local currencies are highly volatile, foreign exchange access is limited, and cross-border transfers are expensive and slow, stablecoins can be used for receiving payments, preserving value, and transferring funds across regions.

The application scenarios of stablecoins have gone beyond the scope of transactions and have attracted widespread attention.

Philip Kwaw Sebuabe, head of the virtual assets department at the Central Bank of Ghana, stated, "The appeal of stablecoins extends beyond trading; cross-border payments, remittance settlements, and foreign currency asset preservation are core applications." Gillian Darko, Vice President of Strategy at Yellowcard.io, a stablecoin payment infrastructure service provider, shares this view, believing stablecoins represent the region's biggest opportunity in the coming year. Stablecoins can meet the market's demand for reliable payment systems, bridging the gap between payments, savings, and investment. Cross-border remittances best illustrate the value of stablecoins: regional stablecoin remittances doubled year-on-year, increasing from $235 million to $492 million; Bitcoin remittances remained largely unchanged. The nearly fivefold increase in the number of stablecoin cross-border transfers indicates a rise in genuine demand, not just a paper increase driven by rising asset prices. Stablecoins are replacing Bitcoin as the mainstream crypto remittance asset. This is driven by Africa's strong demand for cross-border financial connectivity. Mercy Emmanuel of Flutterwave noted, "Africa has a strong demand for international financial connectivity, but payment links are fragmented by different currencies, markets, and financial institutions. Stablecoins have the opportunity to bridge the value gap between these isolated systems." Against this backdrop, local currency stablecoins are gaining attention. Rob Downes, Head of Digital Assets at Absa CIB, a pan-African bank, pointed out that local currency stablecoins are emerging, with pilot programs in South Africa, Ghana, Kenya, and Tanzania. For example, the Central Bank of Ghana is studying a cedi-backed stablecoin scheme: the stablecoin handles settlement, and the recipient can ultimately receive Ghanaian cedi through a bank account or mobile wallet, without needing to hold the crypto assets themselves. Philip Kwaw Sebuabe also mentioned another major advantage of stablecoins: they are not restricted by traditional bank operating hours. Bank transfers are typically limited by weekdays, weekends, and holidays, while stablecoin transactions can be settled 24/7, which is particularly important for international trade, cross-border remittances, and financial markets. These trends illustrate that stablecoins fulfill two major functions: providing exposure to foreign currencies such as the US dollar, while simultaneously optimizing regional payment systems. The large-scale adoption of stablecoins largely depends on clear regulation. Ghana and Kenya have already introduced stablecoin-related regulations last year, setting rules for the rapidly expanding stablecoin market and supporting wider adoption. Intra-African Encrypted Payment Channels Expand as Businesses Seek Low-Cost Cross-Border Settlement

Research observes rapid growth in business-to-business payments within Africa, with cryptocurrencies playing an increasingly important role in cross-border transfers between businesses in the region. The statistics include payments from consumers to merchants and transfers between businesses.

This growth stems from long-standing pain points in traditional African cross-border commercial payments: only a small portion of intra-African cross-border payments are cleared within Africa, leading to high losses and regulatory friction. Against this backdrop, encrypted payment channels connecting African merchants and consumers have become a highly attractive alternative.

Data shows that during the statistical period, the number of active encrypted payment channels in the region nearly doubled, from 80 to 152, with 95 channels experiencing two-way fund flows; the total transaction volume more than doubled, from $34.3 million to $116.5 million.

The average transaction size per channel increased from $429,000 to $766,000, indicating broader regional financial connectivity and continued deepening of transaction activity. The number of intra-Saharan African cross-border commercial payment channels has nearly doubled. This trend signifies not only a shift in crypto-based fund flows between African markets, but also that crypto payment channels are serving merchants and consumers underserved by traditional financial infrastructure. While regional demand for these crypto payment channels is strong, the ability of financial institutions and mainstream payment service providers to accept cryptocurrencies will determine the sustainability of this sector's growth. Gillian Darko emphasized the role of banks in intra-African transfers, international payments, and remittances; for stablecoin payments to become widespread, they must be integrated with the existing banking system, allowing on-chain transactions to access a broader range of financial infrastructure. North America is the main source of crypto remittances to Sub-Saharan Africa. Besides corporate payments, crypto remittances are gaining increasing importance in Sub-Saharan Africa. Traditional remittances are expensive, making cryptocurrencies a highly attractive low-cost alternative. Remittances are a significant source of income for many countries in the region; in countries like Gambia and Lesotho, remittances account for a high percentage of GDP. In 2025, Sub-Saharan Africa received a large amount of cross-border remittances. However, the cost of remittances to the region remains persistently high: World Bank data shows that the average fee for a $200 remittance is among the highest globally. For recipients, even a slight decrease in transaction fees can bring tangible benefits. Encrypted remittances play a crucial role in this scenario, reducing costs, breaking down barriers, and accelerating transfers. Research shows that developed countries are the main recipients of encrypted remittances to sub-Saharan Africa, with a total amount of $888 million during the statistical period, a year-on-year increase of 36%. The number of transactions is growing even faster, increasing by 43%, and is expected to exceed 1 million transactions in 2026.

The total amount of encrypted remittances from Western countries to sub-Saharan Africa continues to rise

North America, with its large populations of Nigerians, Ghanaians, and Ethiopians, is the largest source of encrypted remittances, amounting to $645 million. Australia and New Zealand saw the fastest growth, with remittances increasing from $48 million to $143 million, nearly tripling; Western Europe saw a moderate increase, from $79 million to $100 million.

The total amount of encrypted remittances from Western countries to sub-Saharan Africa continues to rise

North America, with its large populations of Nigerians, Ghanaians, and Ethiopians, is the largest source of encrypted remittances, amounting to $645 million.

The scale of cryptocurrency remittances is strongly correlated with the number of African immigrants in the country

In terms of per capita outflow, Canada ranks first: the cryptocurrency remittances per sub-Saharan African immigrant rose from $586 to $736; the US saw an increase to $143; and Western Europe saw only a rise from $14.5 to $17.9.

...

Canada has the highest average remittance amount, while Western Europe is generally lower

The differences are the result of the combined effects of the economic and policy environment of the remittance source country, the income level of the expatriates, and the maturity of the local cryptocurrency market. Job opportunities and social welfare affect the amount of funds that expatriates can transfer; the degree of cryptocurrency adoption determines whether people choose cryptocurrency remittances.

North America has a high proportion of cryptocurrency remittances precisely because of the large number of African immigrants there and the maturity of the cryptocurrency market. This also shows that the correlation between immigration and cryptocurrency remittances is highly dependent on the local environment of the immigrant's country of settlement.

South African businesses are widely accepting crypto payments. Research has found that South Africa has developed a sizable crypto-based economy, with consumers and merchants directly using cryptocurrencies to purchase goods and services. The research uses merchant-facing payment data within South Africa: wallet-to-wallet transfers where the recipient's transaction characteristics are merchant service payments. The scope is broad, including businesses using crypto payments for long-term service contracts and consumers scanning QR codes to buy fast food. To exclude extreme large transactions, a single transaction limit of $50,000 was set. This category includes legitimate merchants, P2P traders, and other sellers. During the statistical period, the transaction volume of such merchant payments in South Africa reached $8.34 billion, showing a continuous quarter-on-quarter increase. In the second quarter of 2026 (the last quarter of the statistical period), service-related transfers exceeded $1 billion more than in the third quarter of 2025 (the starting quarter of the statistical period). The growth rate of these merchant payments even exceeds the rapid growth of institutional crypto fund inflows in South Africa, which totaled $1.29 billion during the same period. The growth rate of service-related payments has already surpassed institutional platform fund inflows. The growth of merchant payments is based on the continuous improvement of South Africa's crypto payment infrastructure. In 2025, the mainstream QR code payment service Scan to Pay and the crypto platform MoneyBadger launched a cooperative payment solution, allowing consumers to use Bitcoin at over 600,000 offline stores. As of August 2026, this partnership covered a large number of retail locations. MoneyBadger CEO Carel van Wyk stated that South African users are increasingly using cryptocurrency for everyday purchases, both in-store and online. The company's Q2 2026 payment data analysis shows that half of transactions were under $13, and 87% were under $60; e-commerce transactions accounted for 48% of total payments. "Combined with our observed repurchase data, this indicates that cryptocurrency is integrating into the daily consumption habits of locals." South Africa: A Crypto Hub in Sub-Saharan Africa South Africa has long been a gateway for international investment in Africa, boasting the Johannesburg Stock Exchange, a mature banking system, a complete industrial sector, and stable trade links across Africa, supporting the flow of physical capital throughout the continent. Chainalysis data shows that South Africa is also a hub for cross-border cryptocurrency fund flows in Africa. To verify whether the flow of crypto funds from South Africa matches traditional economic and trade relations, the team compared the flow of crypto cross-border payments and foreign direct investment (FDI) from South Africa: South Africa has long been a core source of FDI within Africa. Crypto funds flowing from South Africa to Nigeria, Kenya, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Tanzania, Namibia, and Zimbabwe highly overlap with traditional FDI flows, indicating that there is some overlap between crypto fund channels and traditional investment channels, relying on established commercial and economic relations.

South Africa's Crypto Payment and Investment Landscape in the African Region

However, the overlap is not entirely consistent. Botswana and Zambia receive large amounts of FDI from South Africa, but relatively little crypto funds from South Africa; Senegal and Cameroon are the opposite. This indicates that the flow of crypto funds is only partially related to traditional outward investment.
